summary: Pad+ma la studied under Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche and Dudjom Rinpoche.
Ármin Vámbéry was a scholar of Iranian, Central Asian, and linguistics. He served as Professor of Oriental Languages at Eötvös Loránd University from 1865 and held a post at Nyugat.

Ènver Ahmedovič Makaev specialized in linguistics and Indology, studying at Moscow State University (until 1937) and Moscow State Linguistic University (~1934–1938). He taught at Moscow State University (1938–1960) and was a professor at the Institute of Linguistics (1954–1976).
Édouard Biot was a Sinologist who studied under Jean-Pierre Abel-Rémusat and Stanislas Julien.

Sinologist and Buddhist scholar Édouard Chavannes studied at the École Normale Supérieure, Collège de France, and INALCO under Marquis d'Hervey de Saint-Denys and Maurice Jametel. He served as Professor at the Collège de France (1893–1918).

Scholar of Sinology, Buddhist studies, and linguistics, Édouard Huber studied in Vienna and Paris under Sylvain Lévi and Édouard Chavannes, among others. He was a department director at EFEO (1901–1905) and professor at the Sorbonne (1912–1914).
Indologist Édouard Lancereau studied under Eugène Burnouf from ~1845 to 1852. He worked as a professeur suppléant at Lycée Charlemagne and as a correcteur at the Imprimerie Nationale (~1853–1886).
Sinologist Édouard Specht studied under Jean-Pierre-Guillaume Pauthier and Stanislas Julien. In 1892, he taught Chinese at the École Pratique des Hautes Études.
Indologist Édouard-Simon Ariel studied under Eugène Burnouf from 1840 to 1844. In 1846, he was appointed conservator at the Bibliothèque publique de Pondichéry.
Élisée Reclus studied at the Faculté libre de théologie protestante de Montauban (1848–1849) and held a post at the New University of Brussels (~1894–1905).

Specialist in linguistics, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and Indology, Émile Benveniste studied at the University of Paris. He served at the École Pratique des Hautes Études (1927–1972) and held the Chair of Comparative Grammar at Collège de France (1937–1972).

Linguist Émile Boisacq studied at Université libre de Bruxelles, Heidelberg, and the University of Paris. From 1895 to 1935, he was Professor for General and IE Linguistics, Sanskrit, and Latin Philology at Université libre de Bruxelles.
Philosopher Émile Bréhier studied under Henri Bergson and completed his studies at the University of Paris (~1895–1908). He later held a post at the University of Paris from ~1919 to 1946.
Philosopher Émile Chartier studied at the Lycée Pierre-Corneille (~1881–1886) and the École Normale Supérieure (~1889–1892).

Linguist and historian-archaeologist Émile Chatelain studied at the École Pratique des Hautes Études (~1872–1876). He held posts at the École française de Rome (1876–1877) and the École Pratique des Hautes Études (~1882–1925).

Scholar of religious studies and philosophy Émile Durkheim studied at the École Normale Supérieure and Leipzig. He held posts at the University of Bordeaux (1887–1902) and became a professor at the Sorbonne (~1902–1917).
Linguist and philosopher Émile Littré was educated at the Lycée Louis-le-Grand (~1814–1819) and the Paris Medical Faculty (~1822–1830).
Indologist Émile Senart studied at Göttingen and Munich under Theodor Benfey and Martin Haug. He served as president of the Société Asiatique (1908–1928) and as a professor at the Collège de France.

Indologist and linguist Émile-Louis Burnouf studied at the École Normale Supérieure, University of Paris, and École française d'Athènes. He taught at Nancy (1854–1867) and directed the École française d'Athènes (1867–1875).

Indologist and linguist Émilie Aussant studied under Georges-Jean Pinault. She was affiliated with Paris Diderot University (attested 2014) and became Professeur des Universités at Sorbonne Nouvelle University in 2022.
